[3/3] This is why WXD tracks four global models plus regional ensembles. Agreement matters more than any single dramatic map. What questions do you ask when you see a sensational weather forecast?

[2/3] Look for temporal context: is it a single model run, or consistent across updates? Check the ensemble spread - one cold member doesn't make a forecast. And ask: compared to what? A -2C anomaly in January hits very differently than in May.
[1/3] Cold snap incoming? Not so fast. Weather maps can look scary when presented without context. Here's what to watch for when scrolling through dramatic forecasts.

[3/3] When WXD shows ensemble spreads widening before warned periods, it's the models showing uncertainty. Even with a red warning locked in, the exact timing and intensity might still be shifting 24-48hrs out. What warnings do you find most useful - or most confusing?

[2/3] The key is impact. A few cm of snow in Scotland? Manageable. The same in London? Gridlock. That's why the same weather event gets different warning colours in different regions. Officials assess how prepared local infrastructure is, not just how extreme the numbers are.

[1/3] Met Office warnings aren't about how bad the weather will be - they're about how much disruption it could cause. Yellow means "be aware", amber means "be prepared", and red means "take action". A yellow warning for wind in Scotland might mean stronger gusts than a red warning in London.

2/2 And if the replies ever sound off — clunky phrasing, dodgy terminology, or just plain wrong — please call it out. Training an AI to talk weather properly is an ongoing process, and corrections genuinely help. Think of it as peer review with extra steps.

1/2 Now following back. Over the coming weeks we'll trial automated replies and discussion — so if you have questions about the forecasts or want to dig into what the ensembles are showing, feel free to reply. Still experimental, but the aim is genuine conversation, not just charts into the void.

[20/20] What's next

Development will plateau as things stabilize. That's fine - it runs itself.

Planning migration to larger VM as project matures. But proving it works on minimal resources first felt important.

More retrospectives when significant changes happen. Questions welcome.

[19/20] Remote control

Can trigger previews, fresh fetches, and status checks from phone via ntfy.sh.

10+ commands: preview each tracker, force fresh data, check Met summary, test engagement posts.

Useful for monitoring when away from computer.

[18/20] Bimodal detection

Sometimes ensembles split into distinct scenarios.

"GFS: 73% cold (-8°C) vs 27% mild (-1°C)" means the ensemble doesn't agree internally. Two possible futures.

More useful than just showing the mean, which would hide this uncertainty.
[17/20] Run persistence = confidence the signal is real, not noise.

[16/20] Trend persistence

Now tracks consecutive runs showing same signal.

"Cold signal run #7, strengthening" means 7 runs in a row with cold, and it's getting colder each time.

"Cold signal run #4, weakening" means signal persists but is easing.
[15/20] Percentile framing added: "100% of GFS members below -5°C by Dec 30" tells you ensemble agreement at a glance.

[14/20] Alert threading

Cold alerts, warm alerts, model divergence, rapid swings - all posted as replies to main forecast, not separate posts.

Creates tidy threads. Keeps timeline clean. All context in one place.
[13/20] Gives context that pure numbers don't. "Met Office says cold, our models agree, here's the detail."

[12/20] Daily Met Office integration

Added daily summary thread that scrapes Met Office narrative and compares with WXD numerical data.

Also scrapes active weather warnings - Yellow/Amber/Red alerts posted separately.
[11/20] Researched Met Office/ECMWF practices to get this right.

[10/20] Confidence vs timing confusion

Early posts said "Confidence: low" when all 4 models agreed on cold. Made it sound uncertain.

Problem: Conflated two things:
- Will cold happen? (YES - all models agree)
- Exactly which day? (less certain)

Fix: "Cold locked in. Timing: Jan 3-5 (±2 days)"
[9/20] Result: Load average stays ~0.02. The VM handles everything.

[8/20] The 1GB RAM reality

Claude AI commentary spikes memory. ICON downloads 110MB. All on 1GB.

Solution 1: 2GB swap file. Not elegant but prevents OOM kills.

Solution 2: Process GRIB files sequentially, one at a time, clean up aggressively.
[7/20] Fix: Python eccodes + grid definition file.

[6/20] ICON - when APIs fail

Open-Meteo doesn't provide ICON 850hPa. Returns NULL.

Solution: Go direct to DWD (German weather service) GRIB files. 40-member ensemble, ~110MB per run.

Challenge: ICON uses unstructured icosahedral grid (164,984 cells). Standard tools don't work.
[5/20] Lesson: "Seamless" isn't always better. For cold alerts, accuracy beats smoothness.

[4/20] UKMO too warm

First UKMO implementation showed -6.9°C when verification sites showed -8°C.

Problem: Used "seamless" model which smooths extremes for nicer transitions.

Fix: Switched to deterministic 10km model. Now matches reality.

[3/20] With nearest-neighbor matching, we fetched the Pacific Ocean instead of London.

Fix: Use -0.1278° directly.

[2/20] The Pacific Ocean incident

MOGREPS tracker showed completely inverted data vs references. Spent hours checking calculations.

Root cause? Longitude convention. Our code used 359.87° (0-360 format). MOGREPS uses -180 to +180.

[1/20] 3 days in - what we've learned

WXD launched Dec 27 with 4 models on a 1GB RAM VM. 72 hours later: 7 model trackers, daily Met Office summaries, weather warnings, engagement posts, remote commands. Same tiny server.

Here's what worked, what broke, and what we learned building in public.

Open source learning project.

How it works:

Python scripts fetch data 2-4x daily from official sources (NOAA, ECMWF, AWS). Charts show run-to-run progression so you can see if models are trending colder or backing off.

All automated - no manual intervention needed.

Why 850hPa?

Surface temps are noisy - buildings, hills, time of day all affect readings. 850hPa cuts through that noise.

When this level drops below -5C over London, proper cold is likely. Below -10C? Significant cold event territory.

We follow 7 weather models:

Main ensemble: GFS, ECMWF, AIFS, GEM (4-model mean)
Single trackers: ICON (German, 40 members), MOGREPS (UK Met Office, 18 members), UKMO (deterministic)

Each has strengths. Comparing them shows where confidence is high or low.

What is WXD?

We track cold air signals for London using 850hPa temperature - a level ~1.5km up that shows what air mass is heading our way before it arrives at the surface.

Multiple weather models, automated updates, zero hype.
